verdicts.trueWording: Robin Hobb has created a number of small intimate settings centred around her characters
verdicts.note: Writers Write page (byline Christopher Luke Dean, posted 12 Feb 2020) carries the quote verbatim, prefaced 'Unlike Tolkien or Brandon Sanderson'; next sentence adds 'Sometimes, they are quite grand settings, but they are always intimate.'

verdicts.trueWording: Hobb manages to make her readers care for her setting as much as her characters
verdicts.note: Verbatim in section 1 'What She Did', followed by the Bing Town / Badgerlock Manner illustration. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Her characters grow or die or get worse. Nothing is stable in Hobb's world
verdicts.note: Verbatim in section 5 'Who she did it for'. The 'rather than remaining stable' limb is carried by the immediately following clause 'Nothing is stable in Hobb's world'.

verdicts.trueWording: The epigraphs at the beginning of each chapter will have historical facts
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the Substack essay (Jeffrey O / jeffreydavidoutcalt, 2 Jul 2024); full sentence continues 'about the history of the Six Duchies, like its kings, landmarks, and culture'.

verdicts.trueWording: A pretty informative, yet boring, introduction epigraph
verdicts.note: Verbatim, placed directly after the block-quoted first epigraph ('A history of the Six Duchies is of necessity, a history of its ruling family, the Farseers'), so the 'opening in-world history epigraph' limb is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: It reads as if we are reading from the same tome he actually scribed upon
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the metanarrative definition paragraph; 'he' is Fitz, the first-person narrator documenting the Six Duchies history, supporting the 'the narrator scribed' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: This should immediately alert us to the potential of an unreliable narrator
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Chapter 7 Queen Desire discussion, preceded by 'there is a lot of bias and malice laced in Fitz's "history" of Queen Desire's death', supporting the 'bias' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: Hobb leaves it up to the reader to do some light investigative work
verdicts.note: Verbatim; the sentence opens 'Rather than waffling between present day and flashbacks', which supports the 'rather than cutting to flashback' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: details about the characters in ways that are NOT disclosed anywhere else in the book
verdicts.note: Verbatim. Page says 'All these epigraphs raise very important details...' of the chapter 9, 13 and 14 epigraphs; the claim's weaker 'some epigraphs' is a subset and is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the slow congealing of fact and fiction in the epigraphs
verdicts.note: Verbatim, in the paragraph following the Chapter 7 analysis; 'congealing ... in the epigraphs' supports the 'across the sequence of epigraphs' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: Hobb uses an unremitting rhythm of buts at all levels of the story
verdicts.note: Verbatim under the heading 'Making Lyrical Fantasy Interesting' in M Harold Page's Black Gate dissection of Fool's Assassin (9 Feb 2016), with the parenthetical '(note the single "t")' and the fractal-buts examples.

verdicts.trueWording: a death resulting from the Thriller has domestic and child-rearing implications
verdicts.note: Verbatim under 'First Person Slow Burn Thriller', introduced by 'She braids the plots together. For example,'.

verdicts.trueWording: the same duty manifests both domestically and politically
verdicts.note: Verbatim under 'First Person Slow Burn Thriller': 'She uses themes like duty, friendship, love and self-determination to link both plots, not just thematically but also practically: the same duty manifests both domestically and politically.'

verdicts.trueWording: She only delivers description when it's part of a conflict
verdicts.note: Verbatim under 'Making Lyrical Fantasy Interesting'; the claim's 'only ... when it is part of a conflict' matches the page word for word, followed by the trousers / party / steam-room examples.

verdicts.trueWording: Hobb always serves up characterisation when it is immediately significant to choices or tactics
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim, but the page says 'always ... when', not 'only ... when' — the converse. Page reserves the restrictive 'only' for description in the very next bullet ('She only delivers description when it's part of a conflict'), so the contrast is deliberate and the claim's 'only' is not on the page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the restrictive 'only' — the page asserts 'always serves up characterisation when it is immediately significant', which does not exclude characterisation at other moments
